title: Why More Grown-Up Kids Are Living With Their Parents—and Parents Are Helping Pay the Bills
summary: Imagine being 39 years old and still living with your parents. That's the reality for Mabel Lago's son. Mabel and her husband are in their 70s and just moved from New Jersey to South Carolina. But they didn't go alone—their younger son came too, because he couldn't afford to live on his own. He worked at a liquor store for low pay and has Type 1 diabetes, which made his health insurance super expensive. 'The young people have really been shafted, big time, with the economy, with the cost of living,' Mabel said. And she's not alone. A huge number of parents are helping their grown-up kids. In fact, about 20% of 25- to 34-year-olds now live with their parents—that's almost double what it was in 2005. An AARP survey found that 75% of parents help support their adult children in some way, from paying for cellphones and Wi-Fi to giving cash for rent. On average, that adds up to $7,000 a year! Why is this happening? Prices for housing, food, and energy have shot up, and it's harder for young adults to find good jobs, pay for college, or buy a home. Mabel and her husband even gave part of their land to their older son, 43, so he could build a house next door. They're happy to help, but they have to watch their own spending carefully—they've cut back on driving and stopped eating beef. Mabel says she never planned for this when her kids were born, but now she has to. It's a big change from when their parents were young, and it shows how tough money stuff has gotten for many families.
why_it_matters: This story shows that money problems are so big today that families have to work together in new ways, even if it means grown-up kids stay home longer.

background_read: In the past, it was very common for grown-up children to move out and live on their own, but today rising housing prices make that much harder.
AARP (the huge group that speaks for older Americans) has found that many parents now regularly give money to their adult kids for things like Wi-Fi, cellphones, or food.

In some countries, like Italy or Japan, it's normal for several generations to live together under one roof. In America this used to be unusual, but it is becoming more common again as life gets more expensive.
Article_Structure: WHO: Mabel Lago (in her 70s) and her husband, their two adult sons (one 39 and one 43), and millions of other American families.
WHAT: A growing number of adult children are living with their parents. Parents help pay their bills, give them land, or let them stay at home because the children can't afford to live on their own.
WHERE: In the United States – from New Jersey to South Carolina, and in towns and cities across the country.
WHY: Prices for housing, food, and energy have shot up. Young adults find it harder to get good-paying jobs, pay for college, or buy a home, so they need more help from their families.

perspectives.description: Parents are showing deep care by helping their children get through tough times. Family bonds become even stronger when people share a home and resources.
It's a sad sign that the economy is failing young people. A full-time job should be enough to rent an apartment, but for many that's no longer true.
Living with parents was normal for most of history. This trend isn't strange—it's actually a return to how families used to work before the 20th century.
